btw on lots of slavic languages kletka means "cage"

btw bottles as currency is reference to how at the times right around ussr collapsed, unemployed alcoholics (most of the working people that lost their job due to economical shock) were earning cash by picking up glass bottles from the streets and giving those away to recycling for payment, system had existed for a while and wasn't anything notable until it started generating more income than the factory job

It's a game based on samosbor universe. So the lore of this universe is basically someday you, and all others citizens of USSR wake up in a infinite soviet apartment building called Gigahrush', and sometimes the samosbor happens. The corridors are filled with purple fog, and all the people who did not manage to hide in their apartments and close the door behind them turn into monsters. After the samosbor, the liquidation team uses rakes to clean up what was left in the corridors after the samosbor.

You guys are playing Kletka! Wonderful!

Here are some tips, and some you discovered already:

Never blindly run down a hallway, always watch your step for traps (most can be jumped over)

Bottles are currency, always collect as many as you can. If you find a dead teammate grab their bottles, break all the boxes.

Meat can be harvested from dead animals and also dead teammates, don't feed meat to Kletka's mouth directly: meat is fuel. Shove the meat into the fuel tank as if it was gas.

Bodies themselves are also fuel! If the Kletka goes hungry because you don't keep it fed, YOU become the food! It will eat you or a teammate that you will have to revive later.

Collect all wrenches, rakes and other weapons you find. Save the wrenches for fixing Kletka bit if you have an excess they can be used as weapons.

There will be certain times when the Kletka can't be controlled and you will plummet for a short time hefore you can turn Kletka off.

During that time fuel and Kletka's "health" will need to be fixed so don't use fuel and wrenches unnecessarily

Unless it was removed, there is a joint that when you skoke it gives you health, they are multiple uses so don't smoke the whole joint unless you desperately need health, the joint will also change the way the room looks

10 days before the one year anniversary of Unus Annus.
The 10 days after my dad died, it felt like a blur of misrememberances and grief. All those days were tough and felt like it all melded into one, horrible nightmare that wouldn't end. Wanting to get away from it all, I decided to check out some youtube videos. On the front page, one year after Unus Annus, was Mark and Ethan's videos on the death day anniversary, kind of like this one.
I watched it and it felt like it was... almost perfectly timed. Like, they knew somehow that I'd been hurting for my father's passing. It was the first memory I'd made after my father's passing, and I watch that video sometimes, just remembering the pain I felt. But I don't dwell on it, remembering the meaning of Unus Annus, and that everything dies and we need to deal with it. It hurts to this day, but I'm not forgetting my dad. I'm not going to go through life with regret, I'm not taking that route. I'm going to be the man my dad would be proud of raising, I felt like I had let him down in that way growing up.

I've watched a bunch of playthroughs of this game and I've noticed that many men who play dont understand how important the last section is in portraying and helping the audience interpret the story. It gives us a lot of insight into the way Jimmy actually viewed Anya - as nothing more than the consequences to his actions, his SA, and the monster growing inside of her. Juxtaposing that with daisuke, there are frequent memorials to him near the ending, like the segment in the vents with his weights and gameboy, and then the grave just before and after his death, and the reoccurring hibiscus flowers. The way jimmy views the men in this story is SO different to how he views anya, and that is explicitly shown, as well as him losing his mind, in the final sequences of the game.

This game is amazing, and honestly i think its full of such dense symbolism and analogies that most people miss all of it. But seeing people completely miss the SA aspect of the story, when its so insanely in your face (the dead pixel on the screen, why medical locks but not the sleeping quarters, anya talking about hiding the gun, anya being nervous around jimmy, jimmy purposefully crashing the ship to avoid responsibility, the ultrasound segment at the end of the game, polle saying "if all of that is true, why are you still so concerned about him?" followed by a "take responsibility" screen showing jimmy thinks he isn't responsible for anyas assault, anya saying "you were right. i should've done this a long time ago" to jimmy right before she offs herself which suggests he told her to off herself, jimmy saying to curly "what would she do?", etc) is pretty sad. it just kind of shows that when you're not familiar with these types of abusive relationships, when you've never been in one or known someone in one, then you just become... ignorant to it and how it affects people.

This game is so intriguing. On one side, the protagonist comes off as a complete monster, tormenting Johnny for years. Yet, the voice acting is so convincing that it’s hard to tell if the guy is losing his mind in a psychotic spiral, or if there's genuinely some Lovecraftian entity demanding annual sacrifices.

This game seems to be directly inspired by Jonan Vasquez's "Johnny the Homocidal Maniac" graphic novel series. In it, Johnny must do much as Ralph does to keep the monster in his wall from destroying the world. Between the fact that Johnny is a main character in this game and that series, the shared premise, and the fact that the evil entity in this game is ZIMforth while Vasquez's most famous work is Invader ZIM, I think the likelihood that there was some direct inspiration here very likely.

The fact it was left pretty up to interpretation if you think Zimforth is a real entity or to just showed how clinically insane Ralph was that he could believe such a thing is such a good ending. Here's my reasons why Zimforth is real though:

The purple color is the biggest argument in Zimforth's favor. I think he is some of god manifesting in the form of purple smoke trail or light. 

- Why would the lamp and TV would suddenly change colors or the fact it's off/on? Johnny couldn't see it, only Ralph too. Don't think these are coincidences, think these are Zimforth's subtle reminders he's always there
- Zimforth's color is clearly purple and especially through electrical equipment it can appear in the form of purple light. After the earthquake, the electricity that can be seen is very similar in color to his appearance. 
- In the other ending Mark didn't do where Ralph sacrifices Johnny, Zimforth's purple light is there in the overhead basement lamp, and vanishes when the ritual is over. The light of the sun from outside shines into the basement to light it, instead of the overhead basement lamp.  This means the overhead lamp wasn't turned on, and was instead the real purple light of Zimforth. 

Other notes that I think support the Zimforth theory: 

- If Ralph was severely ill his madness should have started much sooner, it's stated  he had no reason to kill anyone until ordered by Zimforth. 
- Ralph feels any pain or consequence the moment he disregards Zimforth's orders. Ralph had always followed orders out of fear before Johnny, and as soon has he disobeys there's immediate pain and other real-world consequences? 
- Ralph admits that he has never read the Bible, nor was in any church or cult. Which is interesting because an evil god does not necessarily need these to demonstrate his existence. Zimforth doesn't need a bible, a church or a cult to have manipulated weak people please him through ritualistic sacrifice. 
- The greatest earthquake follows from Ralph's denial of Zimforth's command. Before this when Ralph was always obedient for many years, there were no cruel events  such as this at all. A small counter I will concede is I don't know why the earthquake happen 32 hours before when the judgement day supposedly was. Also, the news reporter says, "this is the biggest earth quake we've had in a long while", not "this is the first and biggest we've had in a long while", meaning it is likely a zone where earthquakes do happen (possibly often). 
- Johnny initially thinks Ralph will commit the ritual on him, and Ralph says he has no intention to do so - he only acts on Zimforth's list. Also you don't need to beat Nightmare to get the other endings. That's mostly just there to make the game more challenging. To get the better endings you must:


Collect all five of Dad's items that are scattered throughout the pizzeria. Each day there is a new item somewhere in there. Once you have them all, enter the party room and the girl in there will drop a photo with which to trigger the 2-Star ending.

The 3-Star ending requires that you do the above as well, but also fix every arcade machine in Jeff's Pizza (and play each one at least once while beating the non-endless ones on the right of the prize machine). Then you have to find and complete all three secret minigames. The first you already found by redeeming your fifth voucher in the past pizzeria, the one with the dog. The others are found by interacting with the gumball machine in the main hallway about 60 times (yes, it takes really long) and by calling Mom from within the party room.

At the end, Markiplier has learned the technique known as "Door in the Face." In the marketing sense, it's about deliberately overcharging a product, but, in reality, you actually lower the price amount (to your actual target price) after people complain about it. However, the goal is to lower it down just enough that the consumers will still buy it even if you're still overcharging it and make a good profit off of it in the process. :)

Another technique is "Foot in the door," where you deliberately charge low and slowly work the price up to your true target goal over time.

Leaving some tips for Mark because despite all the work the developers did to make the interface as intuitive as possible - I see that it is still very confusing to learn for beginners. This is not Marks fault at all. 

1) Holding down "I" will pull up your backpack, which has its own dedicated quick slots. You can add items to your backpack in your craffting menu. Backpack slots also have varying sizes.

2) Don't just hold down "E" to pick up items because holding it down is consume, not pick up. Just tap "E" unless you want to eat or carry something off the ground.

3) The blueprint system of custom structures is completely reworked from the first game. You must build everything one log/stick at a time manually. Although, there are a handfull of premade structures- they kind of suck. Cannibals cannot climb up spiked defensive walls, so try to get a wall down ASAP.

4) Hit "G" to holster whatever you have in your hand or to quick swap to whatever you previously equipped.

5) You can parry enemy attacks with melee weapons by double clicking RMB, and can also charge up for power swings. 

6) Chop a log as small as you can and then split it in half to get firewood.

7) Hold down "C" to pick up/destroy placed structures.

8) Find and fill a cooking pot with water and boil it to get clean water. There are also a ton of different cooking recipes with various perks such as "Greg", which is essentially throwing a whole human into a pot for the best buff in the game. You can also collect the pot and save it for later. Greg won't mind.

9) The muscle arm logo with the number on it next to your food, water, and sleep gauges is your player level. The more activities you do (cut down trees, fight cannibals, etc.) you will level up faster and become stronger. You take less damage, have more stamina & health, inflict more damage, and cut down trees faster. Its a hidden leveling system.

Hope this helps!

EDIT: You missed the stun gun in the rebreather cave. Well done making it through the zipline cave. Good luck with the shovel cave because its long. I highly recommend bringing extra explosives.

A few survival tips, if you will. 

you can:
interact with red glowing laptops to find new map markers
set up a tent just inside caves to safely save/sleep
throw (fresh) cannibal parts into the water to distract the shark
select any crafting ingredient, hover over the gear marker and see a list of possible crafting recipes.
leave kelvin behind, no matter how far away, he will safely walk straight back to you, even if enemies are nearby, just run and abandon him, He makes his way back. hes only at risk if youre standing close enough that the cannibals are still spawned in/attacking him for too long. he cant be captured or anything. If you leave him at camp he can fill holders for you, but he'll eventually return

I would recommend: 
crafting a bow first 
using duct tape, rope, and bones for bone armor
find an EUC (electric unicycle) for insanely fast road travel
establish a small walled off supply outpost full of holders for sticks, rocks, logs etc, you can order kelvin to fill containers so make A LOT
make some drying racks and hang up food before it goes bad, it'll be edible in a few days time, and winter comes pretty quickly here
find cooking pot for cooking up cans of food
find winter jacket

Leaving some tips for Mark because despite all the work the developers did to make the interface as intuitive as possible - I see that it is still very confusing to learn for beginners. This is not Marks fault at all. 

1) Holding down "I" will pull up your backpack, which has its own dedicated quick slots. You can add items to your backpack in your craffting menu. Backpack slots also have varying sizes.

2) Don't just hold down "E" to pick up items because holding it down is "consume", not "pick up". Just tap E unless you want to eat or carry something off the ground.

3) The blueprint system of custom structures is completely reworked from the first game. You must build everything one log/stick at a time manually. Although, there are a handfull of premade structures- they kind of suck. Cannibals cannot climb up spiked defensive walls, so try to get a wall down ASAP.

4) Hit "G" to holster whatever you have in your hand.

5) You can parry enemy attacks with melee weapons by double clicking RMB, and can also charge up for power swings. 

6) Chop a log as small as you can and then split it in half to get firewood.

7) Hold down "C" to to pick up/destroy placed structures.

8) The muscle arm logo with the number on it next to your food, water, and sleep gauges is your player level. The more activities you do (cut down trees, fight cannibals, etc.) you will level up faster and become stronger. You take less damage, have more stamina & health, inflict more damage, and cut down trees faster. Its a hidden leveling system.

Hope this helps!

Well-meaning entrepreneur engages with powers he doesn’t understand in order to achieve a stupid goal that doesn’t really seem worth it, avoids all warning signs while continuously writing down convenient exposition on sheets of paper scattered conveniently around the disaster sight, only for the entirely foreseeable consequences of his actions to ultimately kill him. It really highlights the absurdity of the standard horror games that we accept for whatever the hell reason.

If you think you'll need that knife, she's someone you'll need to use it on. If you think you won't, she isn't.
In the end, that first choice is the same. Your endings are the product of what you think you'll need.
If you take the knife, you think there's some path in which you'll need to kill her, to end death. And if you change your mind, you still have the knife, and it still needs to be used.
But if you don't take the knife, then you don't think you'll need it. You don't think you'll need to kill her. You don't think death needs to end. And it doesn't.

For people who don't understand (~3 min read, also includes a TLDR version):

The Princess symbolizes change and transformation. That also includes death. Her name is the Shifting Mound (the big amalgamation of all of the princesses). The MC and the Shifting Mound are two pieces that complete each other. They were originally one God, but were separated by The Narrator. The Narrators goal was to create a world without death and change. That's why after slaying the princess, the MC is stuck in the cabin doing nothing. To The Narrator, that IS a happy ending.

The Princess in the cabin is a part of the Shifting Mound. However, the Shifting Mound is not entirely The Princess. Throughout the game, each ending you get gives the Shifting Mound new perspectives. The Princess in the cabin is the first princess you find. The Shifting Mound is an amalgamation of every possible perspective/princess in the game.

The final choices are to slay the Shifting Mound (rid the world of death and change), leave with the princess (leaving the cabin with The Princess), leave with the Shifting Mound to start new worlds, or loop the game forever to prevent the end of the world as you know it. There's no good or bad ending. It depends on your beliefs. I'll go into detail on each ending below:

SLAY THE PRINCESS: This ending is the direct opposite from the "Leaving With The Shifting Mound" ending. This rids the world of death, but also change itself. Most importantly, the MC will have to live an eternity alone. The MC will go on to forge new realities and universes, but why? Is there a meaning to life without death? Should there be life with no change? And if life is meaningless without death, why create these universes where existence is pointless? The ending depends on your answer to these questions.

LEAVE WITH THE PRINCESS: The MC abandons the Shifting Mound and godhood. They forge a new beginning with The Princess in the cabin. The MC and The Princess remain separate beings. They are free to explore this newfound freedom together without the shackles of The Narrator. The Princess can finally just exist without a role to play. I personally see this as the most romantic and happy ending. I don't have much insight on this ending. If anyone has any ideas, please reply to this comment!

LEAVING WITH THE SHIFTING MOUND: This ending is the direct opposite from the "Slay The Princess" ending. The MC and the Shifting Mound leave together. Although they are separate beings, they are able to come together as Gods to create new universes. Endlessly, they create and destroy new worlds together with their newfound power. This makes the player question things. Is it good to keep the Shifting Mound alive? Is it okay to create these worlds just to destroy them in the end? The ending depends on your answer to these questions.

LOOPING ENDING: This is the one Mark goes into detail about at 46:01. In this ending, the MC and The Princess choose to start the game over again. This means that The Princess doesn't die, but the MC dies instead. The entire world restarts back to when you first opened the game. In this ending, everything remains the same as it was before you ever learned the truth. Will you put blind faith into yourself and The Princess to keep choosing the same thing forever? Is it moral to keep this vicious cycle going when it has caused you and The Princess so much pain? This ending prevents the end of the world as you know it, but is it a good solution? Although you could theoretically keep choosing this forever, it's not likely. Someday, there will be an end. I apologize for my lack of insight on this ending. I personally find this one the most dissatisfying. Just as Mark says, everything must end eventually.

There are a LOT of details about this story that I intentionally left out for the sake of simplicity. This game can be confusing at first, so I want to start off with the basics. There are multiple video essays that you can find about this game. Overall, I find "Why Slay the Princess is a Genuine Masterpiece" by PakPak to be the most informative and easy to understand.

TLDR VERSION: The Princess and the MC were two gods that were separated by The Narrator. His goal was to rid the world of death and change. The final choice is dependent on your beliefs. Do you think the world would be better without death and change? Go with the "Slay the Princess" ending. Do you think the world needs change and death? Go with the "Leaving With The Shifting Mound" ending. Do you want to abandon your Godhood and lead a simple life with The Princess without The Narrator? Then go with the "Leave with The Princess" ending. Do you want to prevent the end of the world and keep looping the game forever? Then go with the "Looping Ending."

The Narrator/Echo’s limited number of questions is part of the design, if you want to get all the answers out of him, you have to keep replaying and pursuing all the different lines of questioning.

Which is also by design to encourage doing more routes to see all the different types of Princess you can get.
You get a maximum of 5 per run, there’s about a dozen.

I sympathise with the Echo, in the philosophical quandary that the narrative of Slay the Princess is built around, he plays the role of those who suffer because of the Shifting Mound, Change and Death. In this cosmic play between Gods he is the mortals caught between given the chance to change the natural order.

In this role he is the Fear of mortality and Grief, asking that if you could change the natural order to avoid the pain of loss, why wouldn’t you? 

Knowing I cannot change the way things are I must either accept it, or rail against it in futile denial but in this scenario the inevitability of death is not a foregone conclusion.
I do not agree with his solution, Eternity would become a prison eventually, but for all those who fear death, both for themselves and others, and those who have suffered because of it and would wish to avoid it happening to others, he is their voice in this argument.

He is sly, everything he accuses the Princess of being, he lies, often by omission or half-truth, he cheats like when he tries to override your decisions and will do anything he can to see his goals to completion.
In short, he’s a desperate mortal person who fears the grief death brings and will do anything to spare whatever mortal race lives outside the Construct from it.

It’s unnatural, it’s sad and so very human. I always find myself sad when I see those pieces of himself breaking in the shattered mirror, the hollow afterimage of a being that feared death so much he personified it and tried to have it assassinated facing oblivion himself. He’s resigned, every word laden with finality, weariness and defeat as his fate, the fate of the world and the future tumbles from his grasp.

And I find some kinship in that. I’ve felt what he has to some extent, like everything has slipped away from you and all you can do is wait out the end.

Personally, in regards to the philosophy about the ending, I prefer the pacifistic ending. I don’t think any heart to heart genuine at the end of a knife. Choosing to give up the onus of choice and leaving it behind together, accepting what will be and appreciating what we have, in this case companionship.

In my case I got my ideal outcome on my first run. I started bringing in a knife, trying to talk it all out before suspicion got the better of me.
By the end I was weary of the bad blood and just sought to talk it out, leave the overbearing life of godhood behind and just walk out a mortal, hand in hand, two people finally allowed to sit down and talk, decide to cut the knot and leave it behind.

Edit: Sorry for the heavy thoughts, this story cranks up the melodrama and sophistry in me. There’s a lot to think, feel and talk about in this, another of its well deserved merits.

I believe the reason the endings were so harsh and limited when you brought the knife down to ‘her heart’ was because you finally had the choice to willingly grab the blade. Before, even if you denied it, the narrator would make it appear anyways, so you had to slay her. The narrator is now gone, and you willingly took the blade to the princesses most vulnerable area. So the only options are what you had throughout the game. You die and the cycle continues, or you kill her and it’s finalized until you go back to an old save because the ending isn’t satisfactory and you loop the cycle as the player instead of as the hero. So essentially both choices here lead to a false death that continues the cycle. When you don’t take the blade it’s finally because it won’t be forced upon you like before. So you are entering her heart without the intent of violence for the first time in the whole game. Which allows you to be free with her and actually have a heart to heart.

She is everything, your choices. You are nothing, the chooser. When you are both completed and together, she consumes you, and the nothing dies. When you are completed and alone, what exists is reflections and fractures of you. But the good ending, where you leave together, both incomplete, is the most human one. Because you are finite enough to be something, without losing yourself to everything and nothing. You are not every choice, and you are not the removal of choice, and that is human life.

I think this game is one of the best examples that portray what I mean when I say that video games are still a very underrated medium for storytelling. if your story is revolving around the human ability to make choices you would never tell that story as well through a book, a comic or a movie/series as you can through one that gives your audience the very ability to choose. whether the narrative shows you that your choices matter (like in this game) or that sometimes they don't, it has so much more impact when it's YOU making the choices and not a character out of your control.

choices in video games can very vividly highlight how significant even a very small choice can be e.g. the change in Princess' behavior depending on whether you go to meet her armed or unprotected and how there are routes that you simply cannot acces through one of those. they can also portray helplessness much better than a medium that you simply consume without interaction, the best example I can think of being a moment in Night In The Woods where you try to comfort a friend in an obvoiusly helpless situantion and you get to choose between two dialogue options "You always have a choice" and "You can always choose". it's such a small detail but it doesn't only portray the main character's lack of agency in this situation but makes you FEEL it, as you have to choose between those two options to proceed even though you KNOW it's exactly the same thing and that it won't make any difference. you don't watch from above as a character makes a choice that is meaningless, you have to make that choice, knowing fully well it is.

I find it sad that video games are associated with easy entertainment and treated like a less 'intellectual' medium than books for example, when there are so many opportunities coming with the ability to interact with the world someone has created for you to not just watch or read about but experience. I hope this prejudice fades in the future and people realize that a good game can be a FAR more valuable experience than many other works of culture and popculture. Slay the Princess is a masterpiece and an incredible example that there are stories that you can only tell by giving the audience the ability to decide where it goes for their own.

Hi! I’m a voice actor! Most of us LOVE to act, it’s why we do what we do. Yes, we’d like to be compensated for our time on projects that will actually come out. My biggest advice for starting game devs: make adding VA’s the last step before you release your game!
Most people don’t realize how much work adding voices is but it really takes your content to the next level of your game if you get good enough actors. That being said, the amount of times people add voices early and then the project never sees the light of day is TOO NUMEROUS TO COUNT. Don’t drag along VAs until your content is 99.9% finished.

From the very first seconds of the game I realized that it's most likely a representation of your anxiety and fears telling you what's best for you. Keeping you away from the things that will actually heal you. 

First of all, all the voices are the same. That's because it's all your inner voices. The Narrator is anxiety and fear trying to take control over you, convincing you that if you do what he tells you to, you will be happy. But The Narrator isn't just the narrator. He also wants to be the writer, telling you what to do. It's the same way that fear and anxiety sneakily manipulates you into thinking you should do what it tells you. "I care for you" "I'm doing this for you" But the princess is right there. And what's the logic in killing her? The picture for the game has a heart stabbed by a knife. Hearts are a symbol for love. And The Narrator wants you to kill that. Because love can hurt you. It can bring your entire world down.

Hero is the voice of your reason. He hesitates and thinks critically. It's like when you're thinking to yourself: "Should I really be doing this?" But fear can quickly convince your reason otherwise if it has a good point.

The cold voice is the opposite of the hero. It doesn't care, it sounds empty. And that's because it is. When you feel empty, you don't care. The cold voice is the most easily explained, I think.

The Princess is the symbol of the end journey. The goal. To live happily ever after. When main character gets the princess, he has won, everyone is happy, and the story ends. In every story, this is the best outcome for the protagonist. She is a symbol of what you actually need. It'll take a lot more to kill her because love is very hard to kill. The coldest of hearts are able to find love.

Your reflection is a symbol of how you view yourself (Shocker) Some ugly dark monster that deserves no such thing as a princess. It's self worth.

In the start, The Narrator tells us that the world as we know will end if we don't slay the princess. How does that voice know that?  All he wants us to is to kill the only thing that seems to be the best thing for us. Once we kill the princess (love) we get the cold voice. A broken, empty voice who doesn't care whether we live die or kill the princess again. Because once love has been killed once, you won't ever forget that feeling. And it will always linger on in your mind. "Why even bother if they'll leave us again?" "Why bother life if the world is going to end?". 

That's about all I picked up from it. I did notice some lines like "Is this really what you wanted? Do you hate me so much that you would kill yourself just to deny me freedom?" It goes to represent that fear is willing to hurt yourself directly if it means staying away from love.

Mark, the concept of beginners luck is very real, except it has nothing to do with luck. When you are doing something blind, you're relying on instinct. In those instances, you either just go with the flow, or choke due to panic of the unknown. When you return to a familiar experience, you're now trying to use past experience as well as react to it, so your brain is working on more things to process. You start hyper analyzing all your movements, the positions of things, try to recall what went wrong with the last attempt while focusing on the present, and psyche yourself out.

18:00 this is actually a documented phenomenon. When you first start something, you have no expectations about how things should be done, so you just do your best and when you mess up, all you think is, "well of course; I only just started." But after you've been doing it for a while, your brain builds up all these expectations that end up actually making you worse. I've found that the best way to combat this is to just take a 5-10 min break when you start to notice the quality of attempts start to go down. When you come back from that break, you will be noticeably better because you've lost that "muscle memory fatigue"

That phenomenon of your first attempt being the best and the reat of the video being you trying to achieve that again is a real thing.
AstralSpiff talked about it in a Peaks of Yor stream — the first and last attempts will always be your best. That struggle point in the middle is when you are trying and experimenting with everything. Its the learning period where you constantly take in information, consciously and unconsciously
Those super powerful attempts are your brain applying everything you've learned. Sometimes it works, sometimes it just gives more learning data at another point. The point being: this struggle is a normal thing and you are making progress even when it feels like crap

18:00 My theory about this "phenomenon" : At the beginning, you are fresh, focus and without any pent-up frustration. But the game is difficult and comes a moment (which happens to everyone) when you lose a bit of focus, you're getting more tense, less precise etc. And when that moment comes, you're entering a 'feedback loop' where this frustration feeds your lack of confidence and you start getting more and more frustrated towards the game and yourself, which in return makes you do more mistakes, and so on.

Solution: you have to accept that there will always be a moment during the session where you'll get less good, and that is perfectly normal. I feel exactly the same when I play this type of game.

I saw a post somewhere explaining the "best try is the first try" phenomenon somewhere once. It really is just psychology. In the first try the focus is purely to see how far one can go and to do the best at every little step, with no pressure at all. But during subsequent tries we have the added pressure where we expect ourselves to do at least as good as the first try, or even better since we should have learnt something. This comparison that is often inflated by intense self-criticism means the middle tries when we are learning something new feel the most frustrated. It is eventually when one learns enough that a try with the added pressure goes as good as the first try will one progress past the first try.

Okay so, for anyone wondering, no there's no RNG. What's actually happening is that the physics is pretty meticulous: every material has a specific friction, and rocks are not at the maximum they're just really high. Too wild a change in momentum will make you slip. On top of that, your momentum is VERY specific. The reason he struggled with the wheel was because he was coming in from too high an angle, making his momentum too fast to grab onto it. 

tl;dr no there's no rng, the physics are just complex enough to roughly emulate the chaos effect.

18:05 I’m rewatching this now, and I have to say, that was a perfectly cut sentence right there.

After watching the “I made the game” video for this game.
The physics system is the basic Unity friction system… the exact same as Getting Over It.

I have no clue where everyone is getting all the “it is exact precise momentum or you slip” as the developer was very open about making it a rage game that uses unity assets and already built in physics system from Unity.
The game is you have force on your hands, when you grab it becomes negative force, and everything has different frictions so that grabbing depends on the force you use. But sometimes your hands will wildly have weird large or small force and that probably is giving you the “RNG” feel to it.
It also explains why you can just be sitting there doing nothing and move your mouse and suddenly slide, as sometimes you’ll just get a large corresponding negative force on your grabbing hand as it appears to also be associated with mouse movement.
The faster or wilder your mouse movements are, the more often the jank in the force will sometimes just slide you. But even going slow, sometimes you’ll still get that large force happen.

I’m pretty certain speed runs are going to be figuring out how to maximize the force in your hands to just fly to the top.

The grip doesn't lock perfectly in place, it's affected by the character's physics shifting around. When you grip in place with one hand and fail a lunging grab with the other, the momentum of you coming back down drags on the hand that was holding on, and on very small surfaces, a missed leap can pretty easily drag hard enough to detach you.

I think part of the reason this chapter was so confusing is because of something I call “bubble narrative”; you have a goal that’s presented to you at the start of the game (use the gas machine to lure CatNap to you to kill them), but early on you meet an obstacle (the power goes out), and almost all the rest of the game is trying to get past that obstacle. Two hours later you’ve spent so much time wandering through corridors and putting in batteries that you’ve forgotten why you were doing all of this in the first place.

When you use bubble narrative you absolutely have to remind the player why they are doing these things. If tutorial kid had said something like “one step closer to defeating CatNap” each time you plugged in a cable it would have gone a long way towards keeping you grounded in what you’re doing in the story beyond “walk through hallway, high five green thing, battery go in hole” for two hours straight.

Mark, I think you might benefit from some clarification:

- The purpose of this chapter was to outline the Prototype's control over the toys and the distinction between those who followed him (CatNap, Miss Delight, Huggy Wuggy, etc) and those who rebelled (Poppy, Kissy Missy, DogDay, possibly others). This chapter centred entirely around CatNap, who worshipped the Prototype like a god. He wanted to keep this "church" to the Prototype sacred and to kill anyone who opposed it. And because we the player oppose the Prototype, that means us.

- In the lore, it's explained that the Prototype was friends with the child who was put into CatNap. The Prototype specifically instructed CatNap to locate and kill the player when we entered Playcare, by any means necessary. This is why we needed to do everything we did - change the direction of the gas to bring CatNap to us, so that we could face him in a final confrontation and kill him. Because he failed in his task, the Prototype itself delivered the final blow and made him part of itself, just as it did with Mommy Longlegs.
 
- Ollie explains to us during the game that CatNap stalks his prey and plays with it before killing it, just as a cat does. This is why he was following us the entire time and not actually killing us when he had the chance earlier. He wanted to make it fun for himself and wanted the chase to last. He sicked Miss Delight onto us, he drove the Smiling Critter toys into DogDay, and he even stole our mask to wear us down. This entire chapter was an almost literal maze for CatNap to stalk us in, wherein we were the mouse.

- The reason why CatNap looked skeletal in some parts but normal in others is because of the Red Smoke. The gas is designed to cause hallucinations and nightmares, so seeing CatNap through the gas made him appear scarier than normal. This is also why some of the CatNaps at the end were not real - because we were having to do all of that while under the influence of the Red Smoke.

I hope that clears some things up!

Some clarification: the biggest thing you missed is that unlike FNAF, it is the bodies and organs of the children and former workers that get put into the toys. That's why Elliot had the dead kid's body with some organs and bones missing. So the toys have some parts of their past selves remaining. For example, CatNap's original name was Theo and as a kid, the Prototype saved his life after he stole a grab-pack and accidentally electrocuted himself. His friendship with the prototype turned into the cult-like devotion we see in the game, where CatNap kills everyone who doesn't follow the Prototype, like DogDay. DogDay and the other Smiling Critters were chained up and slowly eaten alive after the toys (which are essentially human remains fused with mechanical parts) ran out of dead bodies to eat. The little ones possess DogDay so they can't be scared off by the flare gun, and he's still alive during that sequence (you can hear him choking on them). As for the Prototype and his followers' motives, they wanted to stop the torture they were going through (children being experimented on and turned into living toys). Although I'm not entirely sure why their plan (kill everyone in the factory, ???, profit) was so. . . bad.

A couple of notes from someone with 100+ hours in the game just in the last few weeks.
1.) the maps arent the only towns avaiable, theyre just the spawn points across KY. Rosewood is the best for beginners.
2.)the map is only in KY because in this universe thats where the outbreak starts. The whole game takes place across Knox county, and the map is huge
3.) clothing is important, certain articles of clothing will provide more protection from bites and scratches, tempretures, and have weight to them, so its important to wear the right stuff when needed.
4.) pick up a digital watch off a zombie, it gives you good info like the current in game time date and temperature outside.
5.) dont run unless absolutely necessary, it makes so much noise and attracts more zombies. Your base walk speed is faster then most zombies. If you feel the need to run try crouching by pushing ‘c’ first. You wont move as fast but you wont make as much noise.
6.) everyday in the early days of your save while tv broadcasts are still happening you can stand in the room with one on the ‘life and living’ channel on at 6:00,12:00, and 18:00 and you can earn levels in certain skills for free. There are vhs around as well that do a similar thing.
7.) important hot keys, h pulls the health tab, i is inventory, c is crouch, v when near a vehicle will open a radial showing you all available options with the car and L will show you current levels in all skills. Books will give you an xp multiplier for the skill for the next 2 levels, starting with vol. 1 for levels 1-2, vol. 2 for 3-4, and so on to level 10

just as a tip for the future tho im sure its alr been said by others. you can use the scrap signs you find like shovels to damage and kill the monsters, turning the ship light off apparently makes the forest guardians less interested in it, if you see a big leech lizard monster then dont panic, it has a big maw but its 90% passive, only biting when you corner it and doesnt even hurt really. the bugs dont agro unless you take items in front of them or from their nest. however you can also use them to save some time if you're feeling bold. all you have to do is open all doors from the console and let the bugs work for a bit, then try to kill them to collect all the scrap. its risky but in some cases its better than going around the whole location. or if someone is very brave and there's a landmine nearby to the nest. start a teleport early before grabbing an item in front and stepping on the mine (hopefully) in time to teleport back and blow up all the bugs at once. then the outdoor monsters are just different senses. dogs sound, ground worm is movement/vibration, forest guardian is sight and i think sound to small degree depending on proximity but not sure. then theres the tusk vulture things. for them its intimidation and numbers. if theres more of you in a group than their group they generally wont try to attack. boombox draws away most of the outdoor monsters too btw. you can use the portable ladders to cross the walkway gaps instead of jumping. when/if you lot update to the Christmas update of the game you should look out for nutcrackers. they can kill you by walking into you or shooting you with their shotgun. when they detect you a eye pops up in the neck to scan around. if you dont move at all then it wont attack, however this is also the only time its vulnerable to kill as you have to hit the eye. maybe get someone to use the shockgun when its scanning so you can hit it. if you manage to kill it then you can take its shotgun. the shotgun is very powerful, you can say goodbye to worrying about brackens, thumpers, hoard bugs, etc once you have it. anyway. if youve read this far then thanks for your time of day ^^

Hey there, I love this game!  It's a fun take on anomaly hunting.  I'm going to try and flag up the anomalies that Mark misses, but it's difficult because he may not show it on video depending on where he's looking.
- 2:46 - the eyes on the poster to the left has changed.

- 14:26 - the doorknob has changed position on the farthest door on the right side of the hallway 
- 15:10 - there is an anomaly *somewhere* in here but Mark doesn't see it.  Unfortunately, neither do we.  Mark's assumption of a "false failure" is not correct.  But the way this game works, you do not need to actually recognize the anomaly to "clear" it.
- 16:14 - when Mark backtracks, you can see a face on the ceiling in front of the Concourse sign.  Mark was standing *under* it at first so we don't see it until he backtracks.  He will fail to spot this anomaly again at 30:31, but backtrack and notice it at 31:43.
- 20:17 - Mark mentions how it's "the one time" he doesn't look at the *back* of the sign... but the front is upside down too.
- 34:20 - Ceiling Face is a wonderful example of how an anomaly can repeat until you successfully "escape" from it.  Mark will not encounter the faceless man again but Ceiling Face is still in play.
- 34:39 - what Mark notices subconsciously is a pattern in the yellow tiles on the ground about halfway down the hallway

The second game is very typical Southeast Asian/Indonesian and I can tell you all sorts of things about the game:
- The noodle packet in the game actually a very recognizable Indonesian instant noodle brand called Indomie and this packet is the fried noodle flavor (Indomie Rasa Mie Goreng), it is said to be one of the best tasting instant noodle to currently exist. Unfortunately, recently the inventor of Indomie Mie Goreng passed away and the food technology community and college sophomores (who would heavily rely on the product) are in grief and would verbally paid respect for her contribution.
- The stomach ache part due to Indomie overdose is hilarious to me since it's very relatable. Many Indonesians would complain the fact that 1 packet is not enough to fill you up, but 2 packets is just too much and upsets your stomach. Most people would go for the "Jumbo" version of the Indomie since 1 Jumbo is more than a regular packet but not enough to upset your stomach.
- The brand of the gas stove top is also very recognizable called Rinnai. The design is exactly like that with the black and brown accents.
- The bathroom is very typical Southeast Asian: Squatting toilet and big deep resevoir to hold water with a small plastic bucket. As an Indonesian, I'm kinda disappointed that the bucket is not heartshaped since the heartshaped bucket thing is basically an Indonesian meme and they would joke about how they can find this specific plastic bucket in almost every single toilet.
- The green plastic chair with that very design is also very typical of Southeast Asian. You can find this kind of chair everywhere from restaurants, sidewalks, to outdoor wedding events. It's usually considered an "outdoor chair".
- The little kiosk are usually called "warung" in Indonesian and it's like a more traditional style of a minimart. Most "warung"s are usually part of the owner's private house, so it's common for people to enter their private homes to go buy something.
- That lightswitch with that specific design is also commonly found everywhere in Indonesia, but I forgot the specific brand name.
- Indonesians are still very superstitious, so the game might be based on an urban legend, but since I'm personally not a big fan of urban legends, I really don't know (?)

That's all I can get from the game. The creator of the game really did a great job potraying a simple Indonesian life.

To reiterate Mark's Fire Department, Police Station, Hospital advice: if you *ever* feel like you are in danger because of an individual following you, and you don't think you can get to one of those places: Grocery stores, Malls, libraries, even fast food places or, if desperate, a School. Places there are guaranteed to be at least a few people around, people who can help or call the police/an ambulance if you need help.

Do NOT go to an isolated location, a blind alley, a forest, an empty street, anywhere you'll be totally alone is a no-no if you feel like you're being followed, you want people around you, because a flash mob of strangers can stop a kidnapper or abuser as well as the closest group of freinds.

After being a victim of stalking, I'm glad Mark is giving good actual advice on where to go and what to do.

Marks advice is sound about knowing where police, fire, and medical is for when you are being followed in your car. Make sure to always file reports of harassment. The police may not be able to do anything, but it goes a long way towards getting an RO by starting a paper trail. Security cameras, camera doorbells, front and rear dash cams, all with sound, are a huge help in proving stalking. Make sure your inner circle and neighbors know. Make sure work knows. If a person shows up unannounced, TRESPASS THEM EVERY SINGLE TIME AND GET THE REPORT. An RO won't prevent a stalker from doing things to you, but if violated, they will at the very least face jail time. Always carry a legal weapon on your person, your phone, a back up battery charger for said phone, and a small flashlight. Make sure to create some last stand spaces in your home that can be locked and that have a bit of water, food, a weapon, and first aid. Work on methods of egress from your home, job, and stores you frequent. Do not keep silent. Make a scene, ask for help, have back up plans to your back up plans, and call the dang cops. You cannot read the mind of a stalker, you can just know they are obsessive, and if they escalate, it rarely goes well. Protect yourself and your peace. Also check all electronics, your car, and home for spying equipment, gps trackers, spyware, etc. Use secure lines only and use complicated passwords. Change your phone number if they obtain it and harass you via the phone. Always screenshot and save messages to a cloud service to be used as evidence if needed. Do not be passive. If there's one thing many stalking survivors regret, it's not speaking up and getting the cops looped in early. It sucks that the onus is shifted on you to protect yourself but that's just the way it is, so be vigilant and advocate for yourself as much as possible. It's NOT your fault, whatever the stalker does, but fault does little to protect you in the moment.

*(I dont think any of these are confirmed, it is just some details noticed, and none are confirmed.)*

*Objective.* In the very first day, we can notice the odd wording like it says "wash yourself" instead of shower. "washing" something usually refers to an object. She probably feels disgusted everyday that she has to wash herself.

*Clothes.* The girl was not seen with any clothes when washing herself, nor did the father even give her any clothes, meaning the girl probably had no clothes the whole time, making "it" easier for her father.

*Kidpad game.* The kidpad game "Freerunner", it shows a small pink square avoiding red ones. The pink square can be the child avoiding her father, who is the red ones. It can also be the father avoiding the police.

*Diary.* The father gives the child a diary in the first day, when we see what the child wrote in the diary, it is noticeable that there are big O's. It foreshadows the really bad ending (ending that Mark got).

*Father's story.* In the first day, the father tells the child a story about a monster he saw, he probably means the police chasing him, or possibly he is the monster, and the child is the one he's chasing.

*Plants.* It says a sentence after watering the plants, "Grow big and strong, little one.", The "little one" probably refers to the girl. But she didnt grow big and strong, because her life was eventually ruined.

*Apple.* The father gives the child an apple, and says "They're best when they're fresh.", which could mean the father likes children better, or it can also mean he likes them if they're cleanz since the child "washes" herself before meeting with her father. According to Greek Mythology, offering an apple to someone means you want to be their partner.

*Chains.* In the last nightmare of the child, we see chains in the basement. Chains can be a symbol of freedom when broken. In the other ending where she escaped, we can see the child breaking the chains, meaning she'll be free. However, In this ending, she did not break the chains, meaning she will never be free.

*Stairs.* Staircases can also symbolize freedom. In one of the child's nightmares, multiple staircases appear, which could be a sign to the girl that she can still find a way towards freedom, which is shown in the other ending. However, if the child chooses to continue taking the pills, the staircases would disappear, showing that she can no longer achieve any freedom.

*Nightmare.* In one of the nightmares, the child sees a monster, being hunced over her, it is probably a warped nightmare of her father.

*Final day.* The final day is labeled as the 147th. If you do math on that, it is about 4 and a half months, which is well into the 2nd trimester of pregnancy whete a belly would be round and big. She was also slowly moving through the rooms because of how cramped they are for her stomach.

The problem with this game is there’s no panic factor.

Jumpscares are an art form that must be neurologically designed. To get someone to scream is not about frequency but immersion, the more a person actually believes that they are about to die (from the brains autonomic neurological sense that we can’t control), the greater the startle response will be. To get someone to actually scream in a game is difficult because:
1) they can anticipate the threat)
2) they must feel invested in their objective, otherwise they won’t be immersed and also won’t feel any actual danger at all.
3) they dont have anything to actually fear, something that can activate and trick their minds self preservation response 
4) they already know its a simulated environment and not the real thing which is why immersion must be the top priority. This is why falling in a VR game for example is a good way to trick the minds autonomic response because it is something we physically can’t control.If you want to make someone actually scream, you’ll have to delve into the science of screaming to actually make it work and make it difficult, you must make it VR first off, then create a longer believable story line that is closer to reality and the threat must be believable, thus way you create the immersion. Then you must induce the startle response from the autonomic nervous system by introducing the jumpscare after long tension is created, such as after the protagonist is being chased, and thinks he gets away. Now in VR, you have for example the player fall off a cliff and then introduce the jump scare, this would be much more likely to trigger the autonomic response because the feeling of falling you get in VR messes with the equilibrium of our inner ear, which is the same “chills” we get when we feel creeped out. It’s connected to our peripheral nervous system which is what makes our hair follicles stand up. If you trigger this feeling by throwing off the equilibrium of the inner ear, then introduce a threat, fight or flight will be produced in the subject and most likely the person will scream if the threat is introduced at that specific moment and the player is fully immersed in the “situation” (not the environment, environment is not enough to create immersion, the situation and objective the player has must be believable as well). The reason we scream is because that is how nature designed us to scare away wolves and other large predators. If done right, the person will go into fight or flight and you’ll get weird reactions, such as startle responses, screams, and people punching at nothing.

It's pronounced Tek-a Tek-a, Teke Teke. It's because when she crawls around, her nails make a teke teke sound. Teke teke, is a Japanese urban legend about the ghost of a schoolgirl who is said to have fallen onto a railway line, where her body was cut in half by a train. She is an onryō, or a vengeful spirit, who lurks in urban areas and around train stations at night. Since she no longer has a lower body, she travels on her hands, dragging her upper torso and making a scratching or "teke teke"-like sound. If she encounters an individual, she will chase them and slice them in half at the torso, killing them in such a way that mimics her own disfigurement.

A credenza is a wide, low to the ground, shallow dining room sideboard with several storage cabinets, typically with no legs, and a polished top which can be used as a buffet table.

In the Middle Ages, it was customary for members of noble families to have a servant taste their food before it was served to ensure it didn't contain poison. The tasting was done at a dining room sideboard buffet table. This table would eventually be referred to as the credenza, which is Italian for "confidence", as they wanted to be confident that they weren't being poisoned by their enemies.

There are actually a few things Mark has missed, including a different ending

Some quick lore: The animatronic locked in the basement, is call "The Mimic." It was apparently the first endoskeleton to receive an AI, dating before the missing children's incident. The reason why it tries to kill Cassie, is because it was in the storeroom where William Afton had murdered his first victims; it observed his actions and mannerisms, and incorporated them into its core processing. This is also why it slowly crept up on Cassie during the default ending, when she tries to power on the elevator. It was savoring the time spent giving Cassie anxiety, like William had done to the original victims. 

As for why it was wearing a costume, that's the whole purpose of the mimic. Its skeleton can change dimensions at will, allowing it to fit into just about any suitable outfit (grizzly enough, even Cassie during the Brazil Ending, when she gets trapped in a corner with the mask on.) Because of how versatile it is, it was used as the base for all animatronic AI in the Glamrock Series, minus it naturally.

Edit: Should also mention, while William Afton taught it how to murder, it learned how to become violent as a result of being attacked by its creator.

Little secrets I've found while digging through the YouTube community for Ruin nonsense:
1. There's a secret ending if you take a wrong turn through the chase scene at the end.
2. There's a secret ending if you find all the hidden cameras at the Pizzaplex and then go through that opened passage in the chase scene.
3. You can find Bonnie if you deactivate all the wet floor creeps (doesn't work yet, patch is apparently coming out soon for that)
4. You can repair Chica if you can find Chica's Feeding Frenzy and win the game, revealing her voicebox as a prize.
5. If you brighten the room where the Mimic (the fake Gregory entity) was being held, you will see a room where these creepy old costumes are held. They aren't animatronics, and from the style they seem to predate the franchise. (Not proven yet, but someone on the site has associated the costumes with the replacements for the springlock suits, as mentioned in one of the FNAF 3 voice tapes. Just thought I'd put that out there.)

You have to think about all the mechanics in this game as if they were a feature at a childrens playplace.  The children are given an AR mask of their favourite character (in which case, Cassie's is most likely a custom job), which includes games, collectibles, and a generally more partylike and techno-ey version of your surroundings.  The rabbit in AR is likely an extremely warped AI that is meant to locate and identify lost children (since the building is QUITE large), then notify the nearest animatronic to come to them, collect the child and take them back to either the front desk or their parents (if they're there).  The child nodes are likely AR switch inhibitors meant to prevent children from seeing some of the slightly less... "faz-eriffic" locations of the building, such as construction sites.  Of course, adults wouldn't have to wear the mask, because the ones that would be there would only be the staff or parents of the children.  Cassie is likely flagged as a "lost child" by the system, which explains most of the animatronics (and the AI's) actions towards Cassie, but it's been a long time for them, to the point of glitches in their softwear and *obviously* missing parts of their body.

When I thought about it like this the level designs and characters made a lot of sense to me.

Given the restart puts Animatronics in "safety mode" (like Freddy was in during the base game) he was uneffected by the virus because it only runs during "showtime mode". Eclipse is likely the default "safety mode" personality because of the fact Sun and Moon are a performance mechanic.

14:52 Explaination :

The way the mask is handled is that there's actually TWO nearly identical maps loaded for each map : the "ruin" one you see without the mask, and the "VR" one you see with the mask.

Putting the mask on and off actually TELEPORTS you seamlessly between both maps at the same respective position (which is also why sometimes the mask is disabled : because it's an invalid teleport target that could get you stuck, like the tubes), but will still display the position of "moving enemies" (like the endos) on the "ruin" map as this pink "digital skeleton" projection you see in the "VR" map.

Funnily enough it also explain why taking the mask off makes you safe from the digital bunny thing : it only exists in the "VR" map, so once you're outta there, you're out of its reach.

Basically, by putting the mask on, Mark teleported to the "VR" map, while the endo stayed on the "ruin" map. Since endos are still given your position and move when you don't directly look at them (Mark was in the "VR" map, not the "ruin" map, hence why he wasn't technically looking at the endo, only his projection).

The endo kept trying to go "after him" but couldn't teleport to the VR map, hence why it was going in circles, not finding any walkable path to Mark.

8:17 -  8:45 This was the only scene in Markiplier's whole Amnesia: The Bunker playthrough which left me flabbergasted. Here's why:

There is mostly no epic music in this game. Not even an epic chase theme when the beasts spots you. In the room with the crazed blind French, there is pure silence. Only the French's poetry is heard. Markiplier had only a revolver with three (or four) bullets and had no choice but to kill his deranged roommate due to his danger level despite his blindness.

And at that moment (8:24), we hear what will be the mad French's last words. And Markiplier, looking at what seems to be his silhouette, points his gun at him. I felt like "Oh my god... It's happening..." and when he shot, the blind French left a painful grunting. When Markiplier shot again, the foe left one last dying scream before falling.

I felt shocked. I had the feeling I experienced it as if it happened in real life. It couldn't believe what happened. Markiplier successfully managed to kill someone with two direct shot with his revolver in a game, the same way someone would do it in the real world, where there little to no people alive aside the protagonist and where the bullets are used for other uses. Only the shots and the painful grunts were heard. No music. Nothing.

I'll never forget this moment.

Mark, just so you know. The reason the monster opened the cabinet door you were hiding in is because you sprinted for it. The monster's AI checks places it heard noise come from, and since you were making a full dash for the cabinet, it assumed you hid inside it because of the noise you were making when you ran. When going to hide somewhere, stop sprinting when you get relatively close to the hiding spot, and make sure you're not visible from where the monster patrols. If a light is shining by a bed for instance, it will be able to see you underneath the bed.

I kinda understand how the monster works. The monster with the unpowered generator wil wander around or patrol certain areas, but when the generator is on and the lights are powered, the monster hides and is stopped from being able to walk around. However though, if you make a loud noise (e.g. your flashlight and falling objects), itll poke his hand out of the nearest hole to check if the player is close to the hole and it WILL kill you if the hand touches you. If you make a REALLY loud noise (e.g. explosion, breaking object) itll come out of the hole and check the source of the sound. If the monster keeps getting disturbed (e.g. coming out of the hole too many times) then his level of aggro will increase and will come out of the hole even if the noise is a little loud like running or charging your flashlight

Interesting note: in World War I, "trench rats" were a real thing. Trenches and bunkers gave rats plenty of shelter...and the countless corpses gave them plenty of food, while also making them associate "human flesh" with "tasty time". Soldiers stated that they could grow to the size of rabbits, exhibited no fear around people, were extremely aggressive (with bites spreading deadly infection), and would *actively feed on defenseless wounded*. Some even said that the rats were worse than the actual fighting, because they would *crawl over people while they tried to sleep*, preventing any chance at rest, and the sounds of rats feeding on corpses in No Man's Land was loud enough to carry over to the soldiers in hiding.

When the war was over, the French flooded their trenches and bunkers with poison gas to exterminate them. It was personal.

On a personal side note: 
My grandmother was a caller many times on the Art Bell show decades ago, she had a life long interest in space, science, and aliens. (Her career was in electronics when she was middle aged, and back then even NASA used to call her to consult sometimes about electronics issues, she was an extremely unusual and whip-smart woman, especially for the 1950's and 60's.) Because of her interests I grew up all my life hearing her stories of alien phenomenon, things like space string theory, and the paranormal. So, hearing an actual snippet of that radio show brought back some memories of my grandmother sitting in our kitchen late at night on the phone calling in, I guess it just goes to show nostalgia can show up in the most unlikely places sometimes. 
❤

I think the problem with head bob in games is that when you walk normally irl, your eyes are focused on a point in front of you, so the sway of your head isn't that noticeable since it orbits around a fixed point. But in games like this your camera moves all around the place as if your character is drunk.

Note to any aspiring devs: head bob does not equal immersion. It’s okay to have a little bit and if you wanna do something on the level that this game has it or really having it in general, you gotta add an accessibility option for it. Head bob can cause nausea and motion sickness for a lot of people. Accessibility options such as this are always great to have. The more people able to play and enjoy your game the better.

I know it's probably a work in progress, but the game could use places to hide in to avoid detection, an item you can use to distract Foxy and an item that helps you escape after being detected by temporarily slowing down Foxy for example.

- Mark's realization of the gold bars at 29:56 was an anomaly that happened at 28:45

Usually this is where I'd post a list of the anomalies Mark missed, but someone has already done that, so I'm going to post some interesting factoids about Mark's runthrough of this map:
- Like all the videos, the editor has done a fantastic job of removing film grain.  Normally this level is one of the hardest since it has a lot of film grain, dust particles floating around, and glare from the light outside
- Mark loses his first round *early*.  Anomalies typically appear once every 15 in-game minutes.  Mark gets a warning for three active anomalies at 45 in-game minutes, which is the earliest one can do so.
- Interestingly, the edited footage does not show any of these three anomalies except for one at 3:55 (the carpet in the Kitchen is gone).  So I can't even begin to tell you what the other two were.
- No, you do not get more than one warning about multiple anomalies.  I think this is to prevent "cheating" by identifying two anomalies but not clearing them, then allowing the warning to tell you when a third one appears.
- As mentioned in previous videos, Game Over occurs when you have FOUR active anomalies.  Mark had one in the Game Room, one in the Hallway, and one in the Kitchen.  Since the game ended immediately when the fourth one spawned, there is unfortunately no way to know what it was.
- At 9:34, there is an edited time skip from 00:20 to 00:53 - this means unless he caught them "off-camera", Mark likely has two active anomalies.  Since he did not get a warning when he catches the picture anomaly at 10:00, it was one of his two currently-active ones.  Unfortunately that means that he will get a replacement somewhere else in a few seconds.
- You do not need to stay on the camera when reporting an anomaly.  In fact, with some intruders this can actually get you killed.  His friends at 14:33 and 39:12 are examples of this - if you stay on the camera too long, you die.
- The camera twitching at 20:15?  If this were the "anomaly type" reporting, that would be a Camera Malfunction.
- On these maps where you just report the room, there cannot be more than one anomaly per room.  Also, once you report an anomaly, it cannot return.  For example, if you clear a picture anomaly in the Entrance, that painting will not change again for the duration of the run.
- Mark is incorrect, it does not "ramp up" in the number of anomalies.  You get one every 15 in-game minutes, give or take (some may be a little earlier or later).  On rare occasions, you can have a second one show up outside of those 15-minute windows, but your current progression does not factor into it.
- Only three anomalies can be "Outside" on this map: Mark encountered all three.

Also, the left-hand rule (like you said) doesn’t work when a maze has loops. Without loops, every wall connects to the perimeter wall. Taking every left (or right) means you’re walking along the perimeter of the maze to the next exit. With loops, there’s a branching wall that doesn’t connect to the perimeter, and following it leads nowhere. This is why, more fully, you are supposed to (1) mark every left (on the left wall), then, if you find a mark, you (2) go right. If all paths are marked, (3) start following a wall that isn’t marked (even if it is along a direction you’ve gone already), and resume as normal at the next junction. Something like this should cover most to all edge cases, I think.

As an example, imagine a 由 shape (assuming the top leads to the exit). If you start at the center facing up, you’ll draw out the top left square, then head down to draw the bottom right square. From there, you’ve gone all four ways in the middle junction. The last rule would have you trace the upper right square to the middle right junction. Then, as you’re out of paths, you follow the outer wall, every path having been taken until you follow that wall straight to the exit. (Ie: (start) ↑, (1) ←, (N/A) ↓, (1) →, (2) ↓, (1) →, (N/A) ↑, (1) ←, (3) ↑, (2) →, (N/A) ↓, (3) ↓, (N/A) ←, (3) ←, (N/A) ↑, (3) ↑, (N/A) →, (1) ↑, (exit). The N/As indicate where it’s only possible to go one direction, eg: turning a corner. The numbers say which rule led to that step/choice.

Either way, assuming you have pen and paper, your best bet is to just map the dumb thing out, lol.

Some information to help people (and Mark even though he doesn't read these comments):
- "Audio anomalies" like what you hear at 16:29 are just ambience.  Their only purpose is to unnerve you.
- The "emergency" warning happens when there are THREE active anomalies.  This warning will only happen once per round.  Game over occurs at four anomalies.
- They do not get more or less subtle as the night progresses.  There are specific anomalies that can occur, and the game will randomly select one of them periodically (usually every 15 in-game minutes).
- If Mark had played more of I'm On Observation Duty 4, he'd know that "Outside" anomalies are ones that appear on other cameras but are located outside (like an intruder in a window)

I absolutely adore this game, for so many reasons. Especially watching Mark play it. The way it builds tension, the way you’re completely left to your own devices, the way it can do NOTHING and still manages to convince you that you’re missing something. It’s such a fascinating experience, the way it takes advantage of the paranoia almost completely fabricated by the player. The psychological mindfuck of not seeing anything, but not knowing if it’s because there’s nothing to see or if you’re missing something, is just so perfect. The brain assumes the worst, you panic, and then you actually miss things. I love it so much

And watching Mark, who has ADHD, play it, is an even more fascinating experience, because the way his brain works is so bizarre and yet relatable, and the way he notices things nobody else would see while missing things most people would catch instantly is just so entertaining. Mark, the Marker projects a "dead space" around itself, causing Necromophs to take damage, hence the red glow on enemies that get near it. The safest place from them is closest to the Marker. The reason for this is that the Marker wants people to gather around it, for two reasons. The first is so that the people might survive and have Marker blueprints embedded in their heads, allowing them to create more Markers, like Isaac in Dead Space 2. The more contact you have with the Marker, the more influenced by it you become. You'll build Markers, activate them, cause outbreaks, and then seek shelter near the Marker you created. This is where the second reason comes in: Markers can only initiate Convergence events with enough biomass, and the death/absorption of their creators. This will allow the Marker to create a Bretheren Moon, the Necromorph Moon from Dead Space 3. The Aegis VII Marker is an aberrant case because its creators were never absorbed, nor does it have enough biomass to fully initiate Convergence. There simply aren't enough bodies on the planet to fuel it. It's trying to create a Brethren Moon, but has no ability to do so. All that it can do is endlessly start and "stop" the outbreak it creates. The Marker is NOT interested in saving humanity; it's using anyone and everyone around it to either create dead bodies for Convergence, or create more "Marker maker" people to spread Necromoph outbreaks to new areas.

It won't be huge spoilers, but as to your final comment at the end of the video, the remake does  good job at framing why convergence doesn't/won't happen in DS 1, but nearly happens, and completes in DS 2 and 3. 

The primary marker(at least when talking about these red ones) that at least started the event or will be the nexus for the convergence to take place, has to be in a relatively select location. When it activates and believes it has found a place and species that is both technologically able to recreate it, and large amount enough of a population to enact a covergence event it will start the process. Initially the marker does most of the controlling, and remains the defacto chain of command, but as more powerful necro's occur, enough for a hive mind to form, the hive mind will take over most of control responsibility. Now the red markers do two things at this point: it either arranges for the architect of this red marker to come to ground zero to finalize convergence (as seen in DS2), or if the original architect is no longer around for whatever reason (the aegis 7 marker was created 100's of years ago, and seemingly the one to have created it seemingly has passed away) then it looks for in the species or race is it currently targetting, minds within that race that are compatible with receiving the marker and it's info within their mind.

TL;DR: The marker of aegis 7 will briefly stop all necromorph activity when put on its position of power, but when it is moved off by kendra, the hive mind regains control. The hive mind is on auto pilot, telling and thinking it still needs to collect more mass for convergence, but the red marker see's isaac as one of the only few remaining sentient things left, and before losing it's full abilities imprints itself in isaac to create the ability for this cycle to continue. This is similar to how Altman stopped his convergence, as he also made a copy of the black marker, and in doing so one of the primary requirements that the marker's could sense occurred, so it stopped convergence long enough for him to try and sink it.

I think the love-hate dynamic of the Marker is because it uses brute force strategies to solve problems. It has tasks to do, and throws bodies at the tasks until it runs out of tasks.

Small-scale, the Marker puts you in a race against the necromorphs to complete the same tasks, but your survival ultimately doesn't matter. It will eventually force you to serve its interests, dead or alive.

The reason why it doesn't simply kill everyone first is because if a living person serves it, then that person could represent a major reduction in time and effort required. It's not economic to wait until everyone is dead first.

However, if living humans take too long, then death will outpace the living, and a necromorph will get it done faster.

Basically it follows a schedule, but is opportunistic about staying ahead of schedule.

- Abyss Prescences are patches of darkness that expand. If allowed to grow, they will overtake the area and end the game. Please take care of these quickly.

It's a phenomenon known as "Light Pollution", basically, the brightness of the poster in the center of the room makes the darkness around it deeper through contrast, thus masking the blood and other textures.
It's also why it's harder to see the night sky in a city with all their lights on in comparison to the country-side, and why your immediate surroundings looks a lot darker when you use a flashlight.
